title: Wanatah and the Palm Sunday tornado, 1965: the weather office had no radar

sources.what: Third tornado of the evening 'had just dropped to earth a few miles south of Valparaiso in Porter County' (about 6:25 pm); it 'would go on to produce near-F4 damage to homes southwest of Wanatah, and would destroy homes near Kingsford Heights.' Table: F3, 'S of Crown Point to SE of Laporte' (Porter, Laporte), 'Several homes and barns were destroyed and 4 people were injured' (no deaths). 'The South Bend office had no radar, nor a remote radar feed. They were relying on phone conversations with radar operators in Chicago.' SELS issued a 'tornado forecast (analogous to today's tornado watch).'

sourcing_note: Sources disagree on the time (NWS and WTHR: touchdown about 6:25 p.m.; Thornton's timeline: LaPorte County at 6:10 p.m.), the path length (WTHR 15 miles, NWS table 33.1 miles), the rating (NWS table F3, NWS narrative near-F4 damage) and the Indiana toll (137, nearly 140, 145), so the short gives no time, length or rating and says 'more than 130'. Temperatures disagree too (70s, 80s): 'unusually warm'. 'Three homes' and the Kutkiewicz farm are the Times's alone, so the narration says 'homes and farms'. The South Bend radar detail is the Weather Service's own account, so it is attributed. The Times has photographs of the tornado taken from a county road; the drawn man with a camera stands for them and the narration doesn't claim it. People are anonymous silhouettes; no injured people or bodies are shown or described. Not a legend: no ghost lore was found for Wanatah. Independent check Nov. 15: the touchdown spot conflicts too (the official track starts south of Crown Point; the NWS narrative, WTHR and Grazulis say south of Valparaiso), so it says 'Porter County'; 'no way to get a warning' became 'Warnings went out, but many people never got them' (South Bend had warned LaPorte County shortly before); 'homes and farms' became 'homes', and Kingsford Heights 'more homes and barns'; trees drawn bare for early April; no full moon (it was about 80 percent lit); palms taken off the churchgoers (palms are handed out at morning services).

beats.text: On Palm Sunday, 1965, a tornado came out of a warm spring sky and across the fields near Wanatah, Indiana.
beats.label: WANATAH, INDIANA
beats.credit: The Times of Northwest Indiana; National Weather Service

beats.text: It was an unusually warm day. Warnings went out, but many people never got them.
beats.credit: NWS Chicago; NWS Indianapolis; Towne Post; WDET

beats.text: The Weather Service says its South Bend office had no radar. It relied on phone calls with radar operators in Chicago.
beats.label: THE WEATHER SERVICE SAYS
beats.credit: National Weather Service, Northern Indiana; The Weather Network

beats.text: The tornado had touched down in Porter County. It crossed into LaPorte County.
beats.label: IN PORTER COUNTY
beats.credit: WTHR; National Weather Service, Northern Indiana

beats.text: Near Wanatah, it tore apart homes. Then it destroyed more homes and barns near Kingsford Heights.
beats.label: NEAR WANATAH
beats.credit: NWS Northern Indiana; Thomas Grazulis; Towne Post

beats.text: This tornado killed no one. But that day, tornadoes killed more than 130 people across Indiana.
beats.credit: NWS Northern Indiana; Janis Thornton; WTHR; ustornadoes.com

beats.text: Afterward, the Weather Bureau changed the name of its tornado forecast. Today we call it a tornado watch.
beats.label: AFTERWARD
beats.credit: National Weather Service, Chicago; NOAA; FOX6 Milwaukee

beats.text: Comment your town, and it could be next.
